When using the optimal policy, when power capacity is available, it is used to charge the batteries, providing more available energy in regions of the route that require more power to sustain the target speed or to reduce the time to increase consist speed to the current target speed. Further investigation of the detailed results for the optimal policy show some additional features. The first is the ability of the consist to follow and maintain the target speed. V. Discussion of Results The first result from this work is the improved computational efficiency of the distance-based LTD computations over the traditional time-based integration. The distance integrations resulted in fuel consumed of 4580 kg and travel time of 6.61 compared to the time integration results of 4615 kg and 6.63 hrs, a less than 1% difference for both metrics. The distance based integration can be calculated 10x faster than the time-based integrations and as result is used for the majority of this work. The time-based integration still exists in the SCORE toolset to serve as a verification for users of the tools on the accuracy of their results. Though other results are not included in this presentation, the errors are always observed to be less than 1% for both with the distance-based integration slightly underestimating both metrics of performance. This small reduction in accuracy enables the rapid creation of trade spaces. The key element added to the distance integration method was better capturing the impact of acceleration and deceleration on the power requirements for the consist traversing the route. In previous versions these impacts were neglected and accuracy was only within 10%. The plots shown Fig. 8 show flows of power sources and sinks along the route for the same consist and route using the optimal powering policy. These plots have more details in them and are not generally made available to end user. Their initial purpose is for debugging the system and the analyses. The top and bottom plots should be mirror images of each other. A secondary purpose is to better understand the power sinks because this can give us insight into strategies for reducing overall energy consumption. The largest sink of parasitic (non-recoverable) power is aerodynamic drag (drag). As a result, finding techniques to reduce aero-dynamic drag may have a significant impact on overall energy consumption.
